summary: This RFC identified the documents specifying the official protocols used in the ARPA Internet, with notes on planned changes. It was a periodic status report for the DARPA research community, and was replaced by RFC 924.

eli5.summary: This is a checklist of which official rulebooks the network used that year. It was reissued often as the list changed.

questions: what were the official arpa internet protocols in 1984
what were the official protocols in 1984
what is the status of tcp
subtitle: Status report of the protocols used in the ARPA-Internet with specifications and implementation notes

tldr.problem: Network administrators need to know which protocols are officially approved, their implementation status, and where to find specifications for the ARPA-Internet.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC identifies the documents specifying official protocols used in the Internet, organized by network level (network, host, application), with status (required, recommended, elective, experimental), specification references, and known issues or clarifications.
tldr.outcome: Provides a status snapshot of ARPA-Internet protocols as of June 1984, including TCP, IP, UDP, Telnet, and FTP. Replaced by RFC 924.

today: RFC 901 was replaced by RFC 924. These periodic protocol status reports eventually gave way to the Request for Comments series and formalized standardization tracks (Standard, Draft Standard, etc.). Modern protocol development and status tracking is managed by the IETF with formal processes defined in RFC 2026 and successors.

sections.title: Introduction and Organization
sections.content:
RFC 901 identifies the documents specifying the official protocols used in the Internet. It organizes protocols by their network role (network level, host level, application level) and provides status classifications: required (all hosts must implement), recommended (all hosts encouraged to implement), elective (hosts may or may not implement), and experimental (only for coordinated experiments).

The document references three major protocol collections: the Internet Protocol Transition Workbook (March 1982), the Internet Mail Protocols volume (November 1982), and the ARPANET Protocol Handbook (January 1978). For each protocol entry, the RFC provides specification references, implementation comments, other references, protocol dependencies, and a contact person for further information.
sections.eli5: This is an organized guide to all the official network rules. Each rule gets a status label: required, recommended, optional, or experimental. The guide tells you where to read the full rule and who to ask questions.

sections.title: Network and Host Level Protocols
sections.content:
At the network level, the RFC designates the Internet Protocol (IP) from RFC 791 as required, noting it is the universal protocol providing addressing for Internet hosts. ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) from RFC 792 is also required as an integral part of IP, used for control messages and error reporting.

At the host level, TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) from RFC 793 is recommended, providing reliable end-to-end data stream service. UDP (User Datagram Protocol) from RFC 768 is also recommended, providing datagram service with port addressing. The RFC notes numerous comments and corrections have been received for TCP, particularly regarding event processing, push semantics, listening servers, and maximum segment size handling, with discussion in RFC 879.
sections.eli5: IP is the main rule everyone must follow, with ICMP as part of it. TCP and UDP are the main ways to send data reliably or quickly. TCP guarantees delivery, UDP is faster but less reliable.

sections.title: Application and Service Protocols
sections.content:
At the application level, the RFC designates Telnet from RFC 854 as recommended for remote terminal access, with the implementation revised since the original specification in the IPTW. FTP (File Transfer Protocol) from RFC 765 is recommended for moving files between hosts, with clarifications needed on data connection management.

Other application protocols receive various status levels: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) is recommended, TFTP (Trivial File Transfer Protocol) is elective, FINGER is elective, and DOMAIN (Domain Name Protocol) is experimental. Debugging and utility protocols like ECHO, DISCARD, CHARGEN, and QUOTE are elective. Gateway protocols including the "Stub" EGP, GGP, and experimental protocols like MUX and Stream Protocol are also documented with their status and any known issues.
sections.eli5: Common services like Telnet, FTP, and email (SMTP) are recommended. Simpler protocols like ECHO are optional. Some newer ideas like Domain Names are still being tried out.

sections.title: Status Classifications and Dependencies
sections.content:
The RFC explains protocol dependency relationships. For example, all transport and application protocols depend on the Internet Protocol. UDP-based applications like TFTP and RLP depend on UDP, which itself depends on IP. TCP-based applications like FTP and Telnet depend on TCP, which depends on IP.

The document notes that protocol status serves to guide implementation priorities. Required protocols must be implemented for Internet connectivity. The RFC includes a note that ICMP is defined to be an integral part of IP, and implementations are incomplete without ICMP. Some protocols like NAMESERVER are noted as having significant problems and should not be implemented further until revisions are completed.
sections.eli5: Some protocols need other protocols to work. Email needs TCP, which needs IP. The document explains which protocols are the foundation and which ones depend on them.

sections.title: Telnet Options and Protocol Variations
sections.content:
The RFC documents Telnet protocol options, which allow negotiation of special capabilities. It provides a detailed table of 26 Telnet options, each numbered, with their specifications, usage status, and which are in general use. The most frequently implemented options are Binary Transmission (option 0), Echo (option 1), Suppress Go Ahead (option 3), Status (option 5), Timing Mark (option 6), and Extended Options List (option 255).

For each option, the document indicates whether it appears in the Internet Telnet Protocol and Options document (ITP), the ARPANET Protocol Handbook (APH), or is marked obsolete. The RFC notes that many remaining options should be reviewed, with the useful ones revised and reissued, while others should be eliminated.
sections.eli5: Telnet has add-on features you can turn on or off, like binary mode or echo. The list says which ones are commonly used and which ones need updating or should be removed.
